content: According to the genealogy in Numbers 26:59, who was the mother of Aaron, Moses, and Miriam?
options: Jochebed
Elisheba
Zipporah
Miriam
explanation: Numbers 26:59 (ESV) records: 'the name of Amram's wife was Jochebed the daughter of Levi... She bore to Amram Aaron and Moses and Miriam their sister.' The correct answer is therefore Jochebed. (2) 'Elisheba' was Aaron's wife (Exod. 6:23), a female figure closely related within the same Levite lineage and therefore easy to confuse (near_passage). (3) 'Zipporah' was Moses' wife (Exod. 2:21), connected to Moses but not his mother — a relational (wrong_scope) error. (4) 'Miriam' is herself named as the daughter in this verse, so selecting her as the mother confuses the roles of mother and child (wrong_detail).

content: According to Numbers 27:21, how would Joshua discern God's will in order to lead the people?
options: By going up the mountain himself to meet the LORD face to face, as Moses had done
Through the priest Eleazar, who would inquire for him by the judgment of the Urim
By heeding the decisions of the elders and leaders of the congregation
By waiting for the LORD to speak through dreams and visions in the night
explanation: Numbers 27:21 (ESV) states that Joshua 'shall stand before Eleazar the priest, who shall inquire for him by the judgment of the Urim before the LORD. At his word they shall go out, and at his word they shall come in.' God's will is therefore made known through Eleazar and the Urim. (1) 'Going up the mountain to meet the LORD face to face, as Moses had done' describes Moses' direct communion (Exod. 33:11), but this passage deliberately distinguishes that Joshua does NOT have that privilege and must go through an intermediary (wrong_scope). (3) 'Heeding the decisions of the elders' acknowledges the role of the congregation and its leaders, but the authority to inquire belongs to the priest through the Urim, so this answer misses the key point (true_but_off). (4) 'Waiting for the LORD to speak through dreams and visions' is a real mode of divine revelation in Scripture but is not what is prescribed here (wrong_detail).

content: According to Numbers 28:26, on what occasion was a holy convocation with a new grain offering to be held?
options: On the weekly Sabbath when the people rested from all work
On the new moon at the beginning of each month
On the day of firstfruits, that is, the Feast of Weeks
On the Day of Atonement, the tenth day of the seventh month
explanation: Numbers 28:26 (ESV) reads: 'On the day of the firstfruits, when you offer a grain offering of new grain to the LORD at your Feast of Weeks, you shall have a holy convocation. You shall not do any ordinary work.' The new grain offering is therefore linked to the Feast of Weeks (firstfruits). (1) 'On the weekly Sabbath' does involve a convocation and rest, but it is not connected to the 'new grain offering / firstfruits' described in this verse (true_but_off). (2) 'On the new moon at the beginning of each month' is a different occasion for offerings in the same chapter (28:11) and is easy to confuse because it appears nearby (near_passage). (4) 'On the Day of Atonement' is the tenth day of the seventh month, marked by fasting and affliction (29:7), and has nothing to do with the firstfruits (wrong_detail).

content: According to Numbers 30:9, how were the vows of a widow or a divorced woman to be handled?
options: Her vow had to be ratified by a priest to be binding
Every vow and binding obligation she bound herself with remained binding on her
Her father had the right to annul her vow when he heard it
A vow was only binding if it was made in the sanctuary
explanation: Numbers 30:9 (ESV) states: 'But any vow of a widow or of a divorced woman, anything by which she has bound herself, shall stand against her.' Because there was no longer a father or husband to override it, her vow was binding on its own. (1) 'Must be ratified by a priest' assigns the priest a role that this passage does not give him — a wrong detail (wrong_detail). (3) 'Her father has the right to annul it' is correct for a young daughter still living in her father's house (vv. 3–5), but a widow or divorced woman was no longer under her father's authority, making this wrong in scope (wrong_scope). (4) 'Only binding if made in the sanctuary' imposes a location requirement that the text nowhere mentions (common_misconception).

content: During the seven days of the Feast of Tabernacles (Numbers 29), how did the number of bulls offered as burnt offerings change each day?
options: Fixed at thirteen bulls each day throughout all seven days
Beginning at seven bulls and increasing daily to thirteen on the final day
Beginning at thirteen bulls and decreasing by one each day down to seven bulls
Fixed at seven bulls each day throughout all seven days
explanation: Numbers 29:13–32 (ESV) lists a decreasing number of bulls: thirteen on the first day (v. 13), twelve on the second (v. 17), eleven on the third (v. 20), then ten, nine, eight, and seven on the seventh day (v. 32). The correct answer is therefore starting at thirteen and decreasing by one each day down to seven. (1) 'Fixed at thirteen bulls each day' correctly captures the opening number but ignores the decreasing pattern — an almost-right wrong detail (wrong_detail). (2) 'Starting at seven and increasing to thirteen' completely reverses the direction of change — a near-miss trap because it uses the same two endpoint numbers (wrong_detail). (4) 'Fixed at seven bulls each day' takes the number belonging only to the seventh day and applies it to the entire week — wrong in scope (wrong_scope).

content: When recounting Korah's rebellion, what distinctive note does the genealogy in Numbers 26 record about Korah's descendants?
options: Korah's entire family was swallowed by the earth along with him
The sons of Korah did not die in that disaster
Korah's line was completely erased from the tribal register of Levi
Korah's sons were consumed by fire along with the two hundred and fifty men
explanation: Numbers 26:10–11 (ESV) recounts that the earth opened and swallowed Korah and his company, and fire consumed the two hundred and fifty men, then adds the emphatic note: 'But the sons of Korah did not die.' (They later became temple singers; many psalms bear the heading 'Of the Sons of Korah.') The correct answer is therefore that Korah's sons survived. (1) 'Korah's entire family was swallowed by the earth' is partially correct regarding Korah and his company but directly contradicts v. 11 — a wrong detail (wrong_detail). (3) 'Korah's line was completely erased' contradicts the fact that they are still listed and continued to exist — a common misconception about their fate (common_misconception). (4) 'Korah's sons were consumed by fire along with the two hundred and fifty men' assigns them to the group killed by fire (v. 10) rather than the group who survived — a confusion of scope among the victims (wrong_scope).

content: In the battle against Midian, besides Balaam, whom else among the Midianite leaders did the Israelites kill?
options: Four chiefs of Esau's line along with their clan leaders
Three Amorite kings and their allied armies
Five kings of Midian: Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur, and Reba
Seven commanders of the Amalekites and the king's counselors
explanation: According to Numbers 31:8 (ESV), Israel killed 'Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur, and Reba, the five kings of Midian,' along with Balaam the son of Beor. (1) 'Four chiefs of Esau's line' confuses Midian with Edom — an entirely different people (wrong_scope). (2) 'Three Amorite kings' recalls earlier battles (Sihon, Og) but names the wrong people and the wrong number (near_passage). (3) 'Seven commanders of the Amalekites' rightly identifies the Amalekites as enemies of Israel but places them in the wrong battle (wrong_scope).

content: Among the plunder taken from Midian, which animal was recorded in the greatest number?
options: Sheep, with six hundred and seventy-five thousand
Cattle, with seventy-two thousand in all
Donkeys, with sixty-one thousand recorded
Camels, with fifty thousand taken
explanation: According to Numbers 31:32–34 (ESV), the inventory of the remaining plunder lists 675,000 sheep, 72,000 cattle, and 61,000 donkeys — making sheep by far the largest category. (1) 'Cattle: seventy-two thousand' is a real figure in the same list but not the largest (true_but_off). (2) 'Donkeys: sixty-one thousand' is also a real figure in the list but smaller still (true_but_off). (3) 'Camels: fifty thousand' is a fabricated figure that does not appear in this inventory (wrong_detail).

content: According to the command, what fraction of the spoils belonging to the warriors who went to battle had to be levied for the LORD?
options: One out of every ten, given to the Levites who kept the tabernacle
One out of every fifty, given to Eleazar the priest
One out of every hundred, given to the congregation to distribute
One out of every five hundred, given to Eleazar the priest
explanation: According to Numbers 31:28-29, from the portion of the warriors who went to battle, 'one out of every five hundred' (of persons, cattle, donkeys, and flocks) was to be levied for the LORD and given to Eleazar the priest. (1) 'One out of every ten for the Levites' confuses this with the standard tithe law (common_misconception). (2) 'One out of every fifty' is actually the ratio applied to the congregation's portion (31:30), not the warriors' portion — almost right, but wrong because the two groups are swapped (near_passage). (3) 'One out of every hundred for the congregation to distribute' is a fabricated figure with the wrong recipient (wrong_detail).

content: After receiving the land east of the Jordan, which cities did the descendants of Gad rebuild?
options: Heshbon, Elealeh, and Sibmah
Dibon, Aroer, and Ataroth
Nebo, Baal-meon, and Kiriathaim
Beth-nimrah, Joradah, and Karnaim
explanation: According to Numbers 32:34-36, 'the people of Gad built Dibon, Ataroth, Aroer...' along with other fortified cities. (1) 'Heshbon, Elealeh, and Sibmah' are cities the descendants of Reuben rebuilt (32:37) — almost right, but wrong because they are attributed to the other tribe (near_passage). (2) 'Nebo and Baal-meon' also belong to Reuben's portion (32:38) (near_passage). (3) 'Beth-nimrah' is indeed a city of Gad, but 'Joradah and Karnaim' are fabricated names or taken from a different passage (wrong_detail).

content: According to the delineation of the borders of Canaan, what was designated as the western boundary of the land?
options: The Jordan River and the Dead Sea
The Wilderness of Zin and the Red Sea
The Great Sea (the Mediterranean)
Mount Hor and Lebo-hamath
explanation: According to Numbers 34:6, 'For the western boundary, you shall have the Great Sea and its coast. This shall be your western boundary.' (1) 'The Jordan River and the Dead Sea' form the eastern boundary, not the western (near_passage). (2) 'The Wilderness of Zin and the Red Sea' are associated with the southern boundary (34:3) (near_passage). (3) 'Mount Hor and Lebo-hamath' belong to the northern boundary (34:7-8) (near_passage).

content: How many cities in total did the Israelites have to give to the Levites (including the cities of refuge)?
options: Forty-eight cities
Six cities
Forty-two cities
Fifty cities
explanation: According to Numbers 35:7, 'All the cities that you give to the Levites shall be forty-eight cities with their pasturelands.' (1) 'Six cities' refers to the number of cities of refuge (35:6), which is a subset of the total, not the total itself (true_but_off). (2) 'Forty-two cities' is the number of remaining cities after subtracting the six cities of refuge (35:6), not the grand total (true_but_off). (3) 'Fifty cities' is an incorrectly rounded number not found in the text (wrong_detail).

content: According to the law of the cities of refuge, when was a manslayer who had taken refuge in a city of refuge permitted to return to his own property?
options: When the case was judged and proven to be accidental
When the high priest who was in office at the time died
When he had lived in the city for a full seven years
When the avenger of blood officially forgave him
explanation: According to Numbers 35:25, 28, the manslayer 'shall remain in it until the death of the high priest who was anointed with the holy oil,' after which he may return to his own property. (1) 'When the case is judged to be accidental' correctly describes the condition for being admitted to the city of refuge in the first place (35:24), but not the condition for returning home — almost right (true_but_off). (2) 'A full seven years' confuses this with the law of the Sabbath year or Hebrew slavery, which has no bearing on this law (common_misconception). (3) 'When the avenger of blood forgives him' sounds plausible, but the text grants no such authority to that individual to release the manslayer — almost right but wrong mechanism (wrong_detail).

content: What sign does the text use to distinguish one who must be executed as a murderer from a manslayer who is permitted to flee to a city of refuge?
options: The act occurred at night rather than in the daytime before the congregation
The victim was an Israelite rather than a foreigner
The perpetrator fled rather than turning himself in to the elders
Prior hatred or lying in wait, or the use of a deadly weapon
explanation: According to Numbers 35:16-21, one who is counted as a murderer is one who strikes with an iron, stone, or wooden object causing death, or who shoves, lies in wait, or strikes out of hatred — such a person must be put to death; by contrast, one who acts unintentionally without enmity may take refuge (35:22-23). (1) 'At night rather than in the daytime' is not a criterion of this law (wrong_detail). (2) 'Whether the victim was an Israelite or a foreigner' is not the distinguishing sign here — it seems almost right because other laws do make distinctions regarding foreigners (35:15 grants asylum to resident aliens as well) (true_but_off). (3) 'Whether the perpetrator fled or turned himself in' confuses procedural matters with the criterion for determining intentional versus unintentional killing (wrong_scope).

content: In the record of the journey in chapter 33, which person is explicitly stated to have died at Mount Hor?
options: Miriam, the sister of Moses
Aaron the priest
Nadab, the son of Aaron
Hobab the Midianite
explanation: According to Numbers 33:38-39, 'Aaron the priest went up Mount Hor at the command of the LORD and died there,' at the age of one hundred and twenty-three years. (1) 'Miriam' did indeed die, but at Kadesh in the Wilderness of Zin (20:1), not at Mount Hor (near_passage). (2) 'Nadab, Aaron's son' died earlier for offering unauthorized fire (Leviticus 10), not at Mount Hor (wrong_scope). (3) 'Hobab the Midianite' is not recorded in the text as dying there (wrong_detail).

content: Besides the tribes of Reuben and Gad, which group was also allotted land on the other side of the Jordan?
options: The whole tribe of Levi
Half the tribe of Ephraim
The whole tribe of Benjamin
Half the tribe of Manasseh
explanation: According to Numbers 32:33, Moses gave to the descendants of Gad, the descendants of Reuben, and 'the half-tribe of Manasseh the son of Joseph' the kingdom of Sihon and Og. (1) 'The whole tribe of Levi' is incorrect because Levi did not receive a territorial inheritance in the usual sense — they received only cities (common_misconception). (2) 'Half the tribe of Ephraim' confuses the tribe — Ephraim was also a son of Joseph but was not this group (near_passage). (3) 'The whole tribe of Benjamin' is a tribe not associated with the land east of the Jordan (wrong_scope).
